questions.stem: Which case follows „während“, „innerhalb“ and „aufgrund“ in written German?
questions.explanation: These prepositions take the genitive in standard written German: „während der Ferien“, „innerhalb einer Woche“, „aufgrund des Wetters“. In casual speech the dative creeps in, but the written exam expects the genitive.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Innerhalb ___ Woche muss die Arbeit fertig sein.“?
questions.explanation: „Innerhalb“ takes the genitive, and the feminine genitive of „eine“ is „einer“. „Eines“ is the masculine and neuter genitive, which does not suit „die Woche“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Statt ___ Autos nehme ich lieber das Fahrrad.“?
questions.explanation: „Statt“ (instead of) takes the genitive, and a neuter noun adds „-s“ in the genitive: „des Autos“. „Das Auto“ would be nominative or accusative.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Das ist die Meinung vieler ___ Menschen.“ ('many young people')?
questions.explanation: „Viele“ does not act like an article, so the adjective after it takes the strong ending. In the genitive plural that is „-er“: „vieler junger Menschen“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich habe gestern mit dem neuen ___ gesprochen.“ ('the new student')?
questions.explanation: „Der Student“ is a weak noun: it adds „-en“ in every case except the nominative singular. „Der Kollege“, „der Mensch“ and „der Nachbar“ follow the same pattern.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Kennst du den Namen ___ Nachbarn?“?
questions.explanation: The genitive of „der Nachbar“ is „des Nachbarn“: the article shows the case, and as a weak noun „Nachbar“ takes „-n“ rather than „-s“. „Den Nachbarn“ looks the same but is accusative.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Wir haben das Wochenende mit ___ Freunden verbracht.“ ('good friends')?
questions.explanation: With no article the adjective carries the case itself, and the dative plural ending is „-en“. That matches the „-en“ the noun takes: „mit guten Freunden“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Alle ___ Schüler müssen sich im Büro melden.“ ('all new students')?
questions.explanation: „Alle“ behaves like the plural article „die“, so the adjective takes the weak ending „-en“. After „viele“ or „einige“ it would be strong: „viele neue Schüler“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Wir wünschen dir alles ___!“ ('all the best')?
questions.explanation: After „alles“ an adjectival noun takes the weak ending: „alles Gute“. After „etwas“ or „nichts“ it is strong: „etwas Gutes“, „nichts Neues“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Er arbeitet als ___ bei einer Bank.“ ('as an employee')?
questions.explanation: „Angestellt“ used as a noun keeps adjective endings. With no article before it, a masculine nominative takes „-er“; with an article it would be „der Angestellte“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich habe mit einer ___ gesprochen.“ ('with a relative', female)?
questions.explanation: „Verwandt“ as a noun declines like an adjective. After „einer“ in the dative the ending is „-en“: „mit einer Verwandten“. „Die Verwandte“ is the nominative.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Hast du schon etwas ___ gehört?“ ('anything new')?
questions.explanation: After „etwas“ an adjective becomes a noun with a capital and the strong neuter ending „-es“. „Neue“ and „Neuen“ are weak endings, which follow „alles“, not „etwas“.

questions.stem: Which completes „Das Wasser im See ist viel ___ als im Meer.“ ('much warmer')?
questions.explanation: One-syllable adjectives with a, o or u often add an umlaut in the comparative: „warm, wärmer, am wärmsten“. A predicative adjective after „sein“ takes no ending, and „warm“ forms its comparative with „-er“, not with „mehr“.

questions.stem: What does „Immer mehr Jugendliche ernähren sich vegetarisch“ mean?
options: Young people eat more food than vegetarians
More and more young people eat a vegetarian diet
Young people always eat more vegetarian food
Most young people have always been vegetarian
questions.explanation: „Immer“ plus a comparative means 'more and more' or 'increasingly', as in „immer größer“. It does not mean 'always' in this structure.

questions.stem: Which completes „Je mehr man liest, ___ wird der Wortschatz.“?
questions.explanation: „Je … desto“ (the more … the more) needs a comparative in both halves, and „desto“ plus the comparative comes first in its clause, followed by the verb. Adjectives like „groß“ form the comparative with „-er“, never with „mehr“.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Das ist die Schülerin, ___ Eltern aus Graz kommen.“?
questions.explanation: The genitive relative pronoun for a feminine noun is „deren“ ('whose'). „Dessen“ is the masculine and neuter form, and „denen“ is the dative plural.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Die Schüler, ___ Projekt gewonnen hat, fahren nach Berlin.“?
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun agrees with „die Schüler“, which is plural, and 'whose' is genitive: „deren“. „Dessen“ is tempting because „Projekt“ is neuter, but the pronoun follows the noun it refers back to, not the one after it.

questions.stem: Which completes „Das ist die Stadt, ___ ich geboren bin.“?
questions.explanation: Being born in a place is a location, so „in“ takes the dative, and „die Stadt“ is feminine: „in der“. „In die“ would mean movement into the city.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Das ist etwas, ___ ich mich schon lange freue.“?
questions.explanation: After „etwas“, „alles“ or „nichts“ the relative pronoun is „was“, and with a preposition it becomes a wo(r)- compound: „sich freuen auf“ → „worauf“. „Darauf“ points to something, but it cannot start a relative clause.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Er hat die Prüfung bestanden, ___ alle überrascht hat.“?
questions.explanation: When the relative clause refers to the whole preceding clause, not a single noun, German uses „was“. „Das“ would wrongly refer back to a neuter noun, and there is none here.

questions.stem: Which completes „___ zu spät kommt, muss draußen warten.“ ('Whoever arrives late …')?
questions.explanation: „Wer“ as a relative pronoun means 'whoever' and needs no noun to refer back to. It is nominative here because it is the subject of „kommt“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Das sind die Kollegen, ___ wir das Projekt verdanken.“?
questions.explanation: „Verdanken“ takes a dative person (jemandem etwas verdanken), and the dative plural relative pronoun is „denen“, longer than the article „den“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Wir danken ___, die uns geholfen haben.“ ('those who helped us')?
questions.explanation: „Danken“ takes the dative, and „derjenige“ declines in both parts: the dative plural is „denjenigen“. „Demjenigen“ is singular, but „haben“ shows the people are plural.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Lärm kann ___ den ganzen Tag verderben.“ ('can spoil your whole day')?
questions.explanation: „Man“ has no dative or accusative of its own, so German uses „einem“ and „einen“. „Verderben“ here needs a dative person, so it is „einem“.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich habe ___ im Park gesehen.“ ('I saw nobody in the park')?
questions.explanation: „Niemand“ can take case endings, and as a direct object it is accusative: „niemanden“ (in speech „niemand“ is also heard). „Niemandem“ is dative and „niemandes“ is genitive, and „keinen“ needs a noun after it, such as „keinen Menschen“.

questions.stem: Which question asks for „mit dem Zug“ as its answer?
questions.explanation: For things, a preposition combines with „wo(r)-“: „womit“. „Mit wem“ asks about a person, and „woran“ builds the compound on the wrong preposition.

questions.stem: In „Es hängt davon ab, ob wir genug Geld haben“, what does „davon“ do?
options: It replaces the subject of the sentence
It shows the sentence is a question
It points forward to the „ob“ clause
It refers back to an earlier noun
questions.explanation: „Abhängen von“ needs an object, and when that object is a whole clause German puts „davon“ in the main clause to point ahead to it.

questions.stem: Which completes „Ich erkläre es dir noch einmal, ___ du es verstehst.“ ('so that you understand it')?
questions.explanation: „Um … zu“ only works when both clauses share a subject. Here the subjects differ (ich, du), so German needs „damit“, which sends the verb to the end.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses „obwohl“ or „trotzdem“ correctly?
options: „Obwohl es regnete, wir sind spazieren gegangen.“
„Trotzdem es regnete, wir sind spazieren gegangen.“
„Es regnete, trotzdem wir sind spazieren gegangen.“
„Obwohl es regnete, sind wir spazieren gegangen.“
questions.explanation: „Obwohl“ is a conjunction, and a subordinate clause in first place counts as position one, so the main verb comes straight after the comma. „Trotzdem“ is an adverb: „Es regnete, trotzdem sind wir gegangen“.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses „deshalb“ correctly?
options: „Es war spät, deshalb wir ein Taxi nahmen.“
„Es war spät, deshalb nahmen wir ein Taxi.“
„Es war spät, deshalb wir nahmen ein Taxi.“
„Es war spät, deshalb ein Taxi wir nahmen.“
questions.explanation: „Deshalb“ is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it fills the first position and the verb must come second. Treating it like „und“ or like „weil“ produces the wrong orders.

questions.stem: Which completes „Er hat die Prüfung bestanden, ___ er viel gelernt hat.“ ('by studying a lot')?
questions.explanation: „Indem“ says how something is achieved: 'by doing'. „Sodass“ gives a result and „damit“ a purpose, so neither describes the means.

questions.stem: Which completes „Ich frage mich, ___ sie morgen kommt.“ ('whether she is coming tomorrow')?
questions.explanation: An indirect yes/no question uses „ob“ for 'whether' or 'if'. „Wenn“ means 'if' only in conditions, so it is the English-led mistake.

questions.stem: Which completes the indirect question „Weißt du, wann ___?“ ('when we have to leave')?
questions.explanation: An indirect question is a subordinate clause, so the finite verb goes to the end, after the infinitive: „wann wir losfahren müssen“. „Müssen wir losfahren“ is the order of a direct question.

questions.stem: Which completes „Sie ging, ohne sich ___.“ ('without saying goodbye')?
questions.explanation: „Ohne … zu“ plus an infinitive is how German says 'without doing'. English uses an -ing form, but German needs „zu“ and the infinitive at the end.

questions.stem: Which completes „Vergiss nicht, deine Oma ___!“ ('to ring your grandma')?
questions.explanation: With a separable verb, „zu“ goes between the prefix and the stem, written as one word: „anzurufen“. The same happens in „einzukaufen“ and „mitzukommen“.

questions.stem: What does „Er spricht nicht nur Deutsch, sondern auch Italienisch“ mean?
options: He speaks German rather than Italian
He speaks not only German but also Italian
He speaks German but not Italian
He speaks neither German nor Italian
questions.explanation: „Nicht nur … sondern auch“ adds a second item to the first. „Weder … noch“ would deny both, and „sondern“ alone would replace one with the other.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the objects in the correct order?
questions.explanation: Two nouns go dative before accusative, but a pronoun goes before a noun, and two pronouns go accusative before dative: „Ich gebe es ihm“. So „es“ comes before „meinem Bruder“.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the correct order for time, manner and place?
options: „Wir fahren mit dem Zug morgen nach Wien.“
„Wir fahren nach Wien morgen mit dem Zug.“
„Wir fahren morgen mit dem Zug nach Wien.“
„Wir fahren nach Wien mit dem Zug morgen.“
questions.explanation: German adverbials usually follow the order time, manner, place: when, how, where to. English tends to put place first, which is the habit to break.

questions.stem: Where does „nicht“ go to say 'I don't know the man'?
questions.explanation: To negate the whole statement, „nicht“ goes after a definite direct object, at the end here. „Ich kenne nicht den Mann, sondern seine Frau“ is only correct when contrasting with something else.

questions.stem: Which completes „Das Kino liegt ___.“ ('opposite the station')?
questions.explanation: „Gegenüber“ takes the dative and can follow its noun: „dem Bahnhof gegenüber“, or „gegenüber dem Bahnhof“. The accusative „den Bahnhof“ is wrong in either position.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly fronts the time phrase?
options: „Jeden Sommer an die Ostsee wir fahren.“
„Jeden Sommer fahren an die Ostsee wir.“
„Jeden Sommer fahren wir an die Ostsee.“
„Jeden Sommer wir fahren an die Ostsee.“
questions.explanation: Whatever comes first in a main clause, the verb stays second, so the subject moves after it. Starting with a time phrase is good style, as long as the verb-second rule holds.
